arguments.content:
Cancer survival rates in the United States have improved substantially over the past several decades, driven by advances in early detection, precision medicine, immunotherapy, and targeted treatments. The overall 5-year relative survival rate for all cancers combined now sits at approximately 69%, up from around 49% in the mid-1970s. That said, survival varies enormously depending on cancer type, stage at diagnosis, age, and access to care — some cancers, such as thyroid and prostate, carry 5-year survival rates above 99%, while others remain deeply resistant to treatment. Racial and socioeconomic disparities continue to shape outcomes across the country.

- Chordoma — approximately 300 cases per year in the US
- Adrenocortical carcinoma — approximately 300–500 cases per year
- Merkel cell carcinoma — approximately 2,000–2,500 cases per year
- Uveal (ocular) melanoma — approximately 2,000–2,500 cases per year
- Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) — approximately 5,000–6,000 cases per year

- Mesothelioma [~10%]
- Gallbladder cancer [~19%]
- Liver cancer [~21%]
- Esophageal cancer [~22%]
- Lung cancer [~26%]
